subtopic_detail: Selecting the test that a chromosomal microarray will not detect in developmental delay
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a developmental clinic reviewing a 4 year old boy referred with global developmental delay. He said his first words at three, flaps both hands when excited, avoids looking at faces and covers his ears at the kindergarten music session.

His mother mentions that her brother lives in supported accommodation and has never been given a diagnosis, and that her own mother stopped having periods at 38 and now has a hand tremor and an unsteady walk. His face is long with prominent ears and his finger joints hyperextend. A chromosomal microarray requested by the general practitioner has returned with no pathogenic copy number variants. Newborn screening was normal and his hearing test at three was normal.

data_table.Examination: Long face with prominent ears, joint hypermobility, hand flapping, reduced eye contact, no dysmorphic features of a recognised chromosomal syndrome
data_table.Investigations: Chromosomal microarray with no pathogenic copy number variants, newborn screening normal, audiology normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Serum creatine kinase with thyroid function and a full blood count
options.rationale: Creatine kinase screens for a muscular dystrophy in a boy with motor delay, and his delay is predominantly in language and social communication without weakness or a waddling gait (Source: RCH Melbourne: Developmental delay investigation).

options.text: Standard karyotype with G banding on a peripheral blood sample
options.rationale: Karyotype detects aneuploidy and large structural rearrangements at a resolution well below that of the microarray already performed, so it adds nothing here (Source: RCH Melbourne: Developmental delay investigation).

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain under general anaesthesia
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is indicated for microcephaly or macrocephaly, focal neurological signs, seizures or regression, none of which is described, and it requires anaesthesia for a low yield in isolated delay (Source: RCH Melbourne: Developmental delay investigation).

options.text: Plasma amino acids and urine organic acids with an acylcarnitine profile
options.rationale: Metabolic testing is directed at regression, episodic decompensation, organomegaly or consanguinity, and normal newborn screening with steady if slow progress makes it low yield (Source: RCH Melbourne: Developmental delay investigation).

options.text: FMR1 CGG repeat analysis performed on a peripheral blood sample
options.rationale: A trinucleotide repeat expansion is invisible to a chromosomal microarray, so a normal array does not exclude it, and the maternal family pattern of undiagnosed intellectual disability with premature ovarian insufficiency and a late onset tremor and ataxia is the pedigree signature of premutation carriers (Source: RCH Melbourne: Fragile X syndrome).

explanation.summary: Fragile X syndrome is the commonest inherited cause of intellectual disability and the commonest single gene cause of autism, and it results from expansion of a CGG repeat in the FMR1 gene that silences the gene when the repeat exceeds about 200. Because this is a repeat expansion rather than a copy number change, chromosomal microarray does not detect it, and targeted repeat analysis must be requested separately even when array testing has been done. The physical phenotype of a long face, prominent ears, joint hypermobility and, after puberty, enlarged testes is subtle in early childhood, so the family history often carries more diagnostic weight than the examination. Premutation carriers with 55 to 200 repeats are not intellectually disabled but are at risk of premature ovarian insufficiency in women and of a late onset tremor and ataxia syndrome in both sexes, which is why the maternal grandparents' health is informative. Diagnosis alters family planning for the extended maternal line, since carrier females have a 50 per cent chance of transmitting the expanded allele.
key_points: Chromosomal microarray does not detect trinucleotide repeat expansions.
Request FMR1 repeat analysis specifically in unexplained developmental delay or autism in a boy.
Long face, prominent ears and joint hypermobility are subtle before puberty.
Premutation carriers develop premature ovarian insufficiency or a late onset tremor and ataxia syndrome.
Diagnosis has implications for the whole maternal line, not only the immediate family.
explanation.pearls: A maternal grandmother with menopause before 40 and a later tremor with gait ataxia is a premutation pedigree until proven otherwise, and that combination in the family history should trigger FMR1 testing even before the child's own phenotype looks convincing.

sources.label: Royal College of Pathologists of Australasia: Genetic testing

subtopic_detail: Oxygen saturation target in established chronic neonatal lung disease before discharge
stem:
You are the neonatal registrar planning discharge for a boy born at 26 weeks and 5 days gestation who is now 38 weeks postmenstrual age and 2.6 kg. He remains on 0.15 L per minute of nasal prong oxygen and has needed supplemental oxygen every day since birth.

He feeds fully by breast and bottle, has had no apnoeas for three weeks and caffeine was stopped a fortnight ago. In air he settles at saturations of 89 to 91 per cent while asleep, and on his current flow he sits at 95 per cent. His weight has crossed from the 25th to the 5th centile over the last month despite fortified feeds of 160 mL per kilogram per day. A recent echocardiogram shows normal right ventricular pressures. His parents live four hours from the tertiary centre and are keen to go home.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148 beats per minute, blood pressure 68/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 52 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 per cent on 0.15 L per minute nasal prong oxygen, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram with normal right ventricular pressure and no tricuspid regurgitation jet, haemoglobin 118 g/L, chest radiograph with diffuse haziness and coarse interstitial markings

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for his oxygen therapy?

options.text: Wean to room air before discharge and accept saturations of 89 to 91 per cent
options.rationale: Sustained saturations below the low 90s in chronic neonatal lung disease are associated with poor weight gain and with progressive pulmonary hypertension, so accepting them to achieve discharge in air trades a short admission for a worse outcome (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Home oxygen for infants).
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Home oxygen for infants

options.text: Continue oxygen at saturations of at least 93 per cent and arrange home oxygen
options.rationale: In established chronic neonatal lung disease the target shifts upward to 93 per cent or more, because adequate oxygenation supports growth and prevents hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, and a home oxygen program allows that target to be met outside hospital (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Home oxygen for infants).
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Home oxygen for infants

options.text: Commence a tapering course of systemic dexamethasone to allow oxygen weaning
options.rationale: Late systemic corticosteroid facilitates extubation and weaning but carries adverse neurodevelopmental effects, and it is reserved for infants who cannot be weaned from positive pressure ventilation rather than for low flow oxygen at term (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia).

options.text: Start long term oral frusemide with potassium supplementation and wean oxygen
options.rationale: Diuretics give a short term improvement in lung mechanics without evidence of lasting benefit, and long term use brings hypokalaemia, nephrocalcinosis and hearing loss (Source: Safer Care Victoria: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia).

options.text: Increase the flow to target saturations above 97 per cent until the growth improves
options.rationale: Higher targets do not improve growth further and increase exposure to oxygen toxicity and to retinopathy in an infant whose retinal screening is not yet complete (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Home oxygen for infants).
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Home oxygen for infants

explanation.summary: Chronic neonatal lung disease is defined by a continuing oxygen requirement at 36 weeks postmenstrual age in an infant born before 32 weeks, and it reflects arrested alveolar and vascular development rather than simple lung injury. Saturation targets change with the stage of care: during the neonatal period lower targets reduce retinopathy, but once chronic lung disease is established the target rises to at least 93 per cent because chronic hypoxaemia diverts energy from growth and drives hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction towards pulmonary hypertension. Faltering growth on adequate calories is often the first clinical sign that the saturation target is set too low. Home oxygen programs allow infants who are otherwise well, feeding and thermally stable to complete their oxygen requirement at home with community nursing support and scheduled review. Follow up covers growth, respiratory syncytial virus prophylaxis where funded, immunisation on schedule by chronological age, and neurodevelopmental surveillance.
key_points: Chronic neonatal lung disease is an oxygen requirement at 36 weeks postmenstrual age after preterm birth.
The saturation target rises to at least 93 per cent once chronic lung disease is established.
Faltering growth on adequate calories suggests the target is set too low.
Home oxygen is appropriate for an otherwise stable, feeding infant with community support.
Late systemic corticosteroid and long term diuretics carry harms that outweigh their short term gains here.
explanation.pearls: Immunise on chronological rather than corrected age, since these infants have the highest morbidity from pertussis and influenza and delaying vaccines to the corrected schedule leaves them unprotected through the months of greatest risk.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Home oxygen for infants

subtopic_detail: Treating a protozoal genital infection and its partner implications
stem:
You are the sexual health registrar seeing a 27 year old woman with three weeks of vaginal discharge, soreness and stinging when she passes urine. She has one regular male partner of two years and no other partners.

On speculum examination there is a frothy yellow green discharge pooling in the posterior fornix and the ectocervix is studded with punctate red areas. The vaginal pH is 5.5. A self collected vaginal swab reports nucleic acid detected for Trichomonas vaginalis, with chlamydia and gonorrhoea not detected and no candida seen. She is not pregnant, takes the combined oral contraceptive pill and has no drug allergies. Her partner has no symptoms.

data_table.Examination: Frothy yellow green discharge, punctate cervical erythema, vaginal pH 5.5, no adnexal or cervical motion tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Trichomonas vaginalis nucleic acid detected, chlamydia and gonorrhoea not detected, urine pregnancy test negative, syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serology pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral metronidazole for her, with treatment of her partner at the same time
options.rationale: Oral nitroimidazole therapy cures the infection, and simultaneous partner treatment regardless of partner symptoms is required because asymptomatic male carriage is common and reinfection otherwise follows within weeks (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI management guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI management guidelines

options.text: Intravaginal metronidazole gel nightly for five nights with review afterwards
options.rationale: Topical nitroimidazole reaches inadequate concentrations in the urethra and periurethral glands where the organism persists, and cure rates are well below those of oral therapy (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI management guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI management guidelines

options.text: Intravaginal clotrimazole pessaries for six nights with a topical antifungal cream
options.rationale: Antifungal treatment addresses candidiasis, which produces a thick white discharge with a normal vaginal pH rather than a frothy discharge with a pH of 5.5, and no yeast was seen (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Single dose oral azithromycin for her and for her partner on the same day
options.rationale: A macrolide covers chlamydia, which was not detected here, and has no activity against this protozoan (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Oral metronidazole for her, with partner treatment only if he becomes symptomatic
options.rationale: Waiting for symptoms in the partner leaves an untreated reservoir, since the majority of infected men have no symptoms at all and reinfect within a short interval (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI management guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI management guidelines

explanation.summary: Trichomoniasis is a sexually transmitted protozoal infection that is uncommon in most Australian metropolitan settings but remains prevalent in some remote communities, so local epidemiology shapes how strongly it is considered. The frothy discharge, raised vaginal pH and punctate cervical erythema are suggestive but insensitive, and nucleic acid amplification testing has largely replaced microscopy, which misses around half of cases. Treatment is oral because topical therapy does not reach the urethral and periurethral reservoirs. All current sexual partners are treated at the same time without waiting for their test results, and sex is avoided until both have completed treatment and been symptom free for seven days. Diagnosis of any sexually transmitted infection prompts a full screen, including chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis and human immunodeficiency virus serology, because coinfection is common. In pregnancy the infection is associated with preterm birth and low birthweight, and treatment is still given.
key_points: Oral nitroimidazole therapy is required; topical treatment does not clear urethral reservoirs.
Treat all current partners simultaneously regardless of symptoms or test results.
Avoid sex until both partners have completed treatment and been symptom free for seven days.
Nucleic acid testing has replaced wet mount microscopy, which misses about half of cases.
Any positive result prompts a full sexually transmitted infection screen for coinfection.
explanation.pearls: Test of cure by nucleic acid testing is recommended at two weeks to three months in women because reinfection and treatment failure are both common, and testing earlier than two weeks can detect residual non viable organism DNA.

sources.label: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI management guidelines

subtopic_detail: Managing provoked vestibular pain after repeated antifungal courses have failed
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 32 year old woman with fourteen months of burning pain at the vaginal entrance whenever she attempts intercourse or tries to insert a tampon. She has no pain at rest, and none when cycling or sitting through a work day.

She has taken four courses of oral fluconazole and used several antifungal creams, none of which changed the pain. She and her partner have stopped attempting sex and she is tearful describing the effect on their relationship. On examination the vulval skin looks entirely normal. Light touch with a cotton bud at the posterior vestibule reproduces her pain exactly, while the same touch on the labia majora and perineum is painless. The pelvic floor muscles are tender and she cannot relax them on request.

data_table.Examination: Vulval skin normal with no pallor, fissuring or architectural change, no discharge, cotton bud test positive at the posterior vestibule only, hypertonic tender pelvic floor musculature
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal swab with no candida or bacterial pathogen isolated, fungal culture negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a further eight week course of weekly oral fluconazole and review
options.rationale: Suppressive antifungal therapy treats recurrent candidiasis, and four previous courses with a negative fungal culture have already excluded that as the mechanism (Source: RANZCOG: Vulvodynia and vulval pain).

options.text: Refer for pelvic floor physiotherapy alongside education and topical local anaesthetic
options.rationale: Pain provoked only by pressure at the vestibule with a hypertonic pelvic floor is managed with a multimodal program in which physiotherapy for the muscle component, explanation of central pain mechanisms and topical anaesthetic for penetration together carry the strongest evidence (Source: RANZCOG: Vulvodynia and vulval pain).

options.text: Prescribe a potent topical corticosteroid ointment applied nightly for three months
options.rationale: Topical steroid treats an inflammatory dermatosis such as lichen sclerosus, which would show pallor, fissuring or loss of architecture, and none of those changes is present (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Refer for vestibulectomy with vaginal advancement flap at the earliest opportunity
options.rationale: Surgery has a place only after a properly delivered multimodal program has failed over many months, and operating on an untreated hypertonic pelvic floor commonly leaves the pain unchanged (Source: RANZCOG: Vulvodynia and vulval pain).

options.text: Prescribe oral amitriptyline at night as sole therapy with dose escalation monthly
options.rationale: A tricyclic is a reasonable adjunct for neuropathic pain but as monotherapy it leaves the muscular and psychosexual components untreated, and the evidence for it in provoked vestibular pain is weak (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Analgesic).

explanation.summary: Vulvodynia is vulval pain of at least three months duration without an identifiable disease to explain it, and it is subdivided by whether the pain is provoked or spontaneous, localised or generalised. Provoked vestibulodynia, in which pain occurs only on pressure at the vestibule, is the commonest form in women of reproductive age and is frequently misdiagnosed as recurrent thrush for years before assessment. The cotton bud test that maps pain precisely to the vestibule while sparing surrounding skin is the key examination finding, and normal vulval skin is expected rather than reassuring. Peripheral nociceptor sensitisation, central pain amplification and a secondary hypertonic pelvic floor all contribute, which is why single modality treatment usually disappoints. Management combines physiotherapy, education, topical measures, psychological and psychosexual therapy, and sometimes neuromodulating medication, with surgery held in reserve.
key_points: Vulvodynia is vulval pain of three months or more without an identifiable causative disease.
The cotton bud test localising pain to the vestibule with normal skin is the central finding.
Repeated antifungal courses with negative cultures are a common and unhelpful detour.
A secondary hypertonic pelvic floor is present in most women and responds to physiotherapy.
Vestibulectomy is reserved for failure of a properly delivered multimodal program.
explanation.pearls: Ask whether the pain occurs with cycling, prolonged sitting or at rest: pain only on attempted penetration marks the provoked localised form that responds best to physiotherapy, while constant unprovoked burning suggests generalised vulvodynia and a greater role for neuromodulating medication.

subtopic_detail: Definitive drainage technique for a fluctuant vulval gland abscess
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar called to the emergency department for a 29 year old woman with three days of worsening swelling and pain at the right side of the vaginal opening. She cannot sit down and has walked in leaning on her partner.

Examination shows a tense, tender, fluctuant swelling about 4 cm across at the posterior aspect of the right labium majus, distorting the introitus, with surrounding erythema limited to the swelling itself. She is afebrile with normal observations and there is no induration extending into the perineum or thigh, no crepitus and no area of dusky skin. She has had one similar but smaller episode two years ago that settled with antibiotics alone. She is not pregnant and has no medical history.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tense fluctuant 4 cm swelling of the posterior right labium majus, localised erythema, no perineal induration, no crepitus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral di or flucloxacillin for seven days with analgesia and warm baths at home
options.rationale: Antibiotics alone treat cellulitis without a collection, and a tense fluctuant abscess needs drainage because antibiotic penetration into pus is poor (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Needle aspiration of the collection under local anaesthesia in the department
options.rationale: Aspiration relieves pain briefly but the cavity refills because the tract seals over within a day, giving recurrence rates far above those of a technique that keeps the tract open (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin gland cyst and abscess).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Bartholin gland cyst and abscess

options.text: Incision and drainage with insertion of a balloon tipped catheter left in situ
options.rationale: A small stab incision with a balloon tipped catheter left for four to six weeks drains the abscess and allows an epithelialised tract to form, which is what prevents recurrence, and it is done under local anaesthesia in the emergency department (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin gland cyst and abscess).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Bartholin gland cyst and abscess

options.text: Simple incision and drainage with a gauze wick changed daily by the practice nurse
options.rationale: Incision alone drains the pus but the incision closes over as it heals, so recurrence is common and this is the near pair that differs only by omitting the device that keeps the tract patent (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin gland cyst and abscess).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Bartholin gland cyst and abscess

options.text: Marsupialisation of the gland in theatre on the next available operating list
options.rationale: Marsupialisation is effective but requires a theatre slot and usually general anaesthesia, so it is kept for recurrent disease after simpler drainage has failed (Source: RANZCOG: Bartholin gland cyst and abscess).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Bartholin gland cyst and abscess

explanation.summary: The greater vestibular glands sit at the four and eight o'clock positions of the introitus and drain through short ducts; obstruction produces a cyst and secondary infection produces an abscess. Asymptomatic cysts in women under 40 need no treatment, while an abscess is drained. The principle that governs technique is that the drainage tract must stay open long enough to epithelialise, which is why a balloon tipped catheter left in place for four to six weeks or marsupialisation outperforms incision or aspiration alone. Antibiotics are added when there is surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy, immunosuppression or a high risk of methicillin resistant organisms, and swabs are taken at drainage. A new vulval mass in a woman over 40, or one that is firm, fixed or irregular, warrants biopsy because carcinoma of the gland, though rare, presents this way. Rapidly spreading induration, pain out of proportion, crepitus or dusky skin should redirect the assessment towards necrotising infection.
key_points: A fluctuant abscess requires drainage; antibiotics alone are for cellulitis without a collection.
The tract must stay open for weeks to epithelialise, which is why catheter drainage beats simple incision.
Marsupialisation is reserved for recurrent disease or failure of catheter drainage.
Add antibiotics for surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy or immunosuppression.
A firm or irregular vulval mass in a woman over 40 needs biopsy to exclude carcinoma.
explanation.pearls: The balloon catheter stays in for four to six weeks, not days: removing it once the pain settles at one week defeats the purpose, because the epithelialised tract that prevents recurrence has not yet formed.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Bartholin gland cyst and abscess
BMJ Best Practice: Bartholin cyst and abscess
